plain: Gradient history is the record an optimizer keeps of the gradients it has seen recently, so that a step can depend on more than the latest batch.
ours: AdamW keeps two running records for every weight: an average of recent gradients (about the last 10 steps) and an average of their squares (about the last 1,000 steps). Muon keeps one record per matrix, the momentum, which at our setting of 0.9 covers about the last 10 steps.
deeper: A running average with factor beta remembers about 1/(1 - beta) steps: beta 0.9 is about 10, beta 0.999 is about 1,000. Two consequences for AdamW. After a sudden drop in gradient size, its squares-record still remembers the large gradients, so its steps shrink until the record catches up. Under pure noise, the average of the gradients partly cancels while the average of their squares does not, so its step falls to about sqrt((1 - beta)/(1 + beta)), which is 0.23 at beta 0.9. These are the textbook formulas applied to our settings; we have not logged them per matrix. Muon's step does not shrink in either case.

quiz.q: What does keeping a gradient history let an optimizer do?
options: Make a step depend on recent gradients, not only on the latest batch
quiz.why: The history smooths and reshapes steps using what was seen over the last few steps.

quiz.q: A running average uses factor 0.9. About how many recent steps does it effectively remember?
quiz.why: The memory is about 1/(1 - 0.9) = 10 steps. A factor of 0.999 would give about 1,000.

wrong.3: 1,000 steps belongs to a factor of 0.999, the usual setting for AdamW's squares-record.

quiz.q: Gradients suddenly become 100 times smaller. AdamW's squares-record has a memory of about 1,000 steps. What happens to AdamW's steps?
options: They shrink for a while, until the record catches up
They stop for the rest of training
quiz.why: The short average of gradients drops at once, but the long average of squares still remembers the big ones, so the ratio is small for roughly that long. Muon's step does not shrink.

wrong.0: That would be true if both records forgot at the same speed. The squares-record forgets slowly.

quiz.q: Why do AdamW's steps get smaller when gradients are pure noise, even if their size has not changed?
options: The learning rate is lowered automatically
The average of noisy gradients partly cancels, while the average of their squares does not
quiz.why: Random directions cancel when averaged, so the numerator shrinks, but squares are always positive and keep their size. At beta 0.9 the ratio falls to about 0.23.

wrong.3: AdamW does not detect noise; the shrinkage is a side effect of averaging.

plain: Momentum is a running average of recent gradients that the optimizer steps along, so one noisy batch cannot push the weights far in a wrong direction.
ours: Our optimizer uses a momentum of 0.9 by default, which averages over roughly the last 10 steps. At batch sizes of 1 to 16 it is what removes most of the noise. Muon takes the momentum of a whole matrix and evens out its directions (see orthogonal matrix) to make the step.
deeper: With factor beta = 0.9 the buffer averages about 10 steps. If the gradient is a steady signal plus independent noise, averaging raises the signal-to-noise ratio by about sqrt((1 + beta)/(1 - beta)) = 4.4 compared with one step. That figure assumes the signal stays the same over the window; if it drifts, 4.4 is an upper bound. The cost is lag: when the right direction changes, momentum keeps pushing the old way for about 10 steps. We have not measured an effect on generalisation.

papers.title: Keller Jordan, Muon: An optimizer for hidden layers in neural networks

quiz.q: What does momentum do?
options: It averages recent gradients, so a step follows the trend and not one noisy batch
It makes the learning rate bigger over time
It stores the best weights seen so far
quiz.why: Momentum is a running average of recent gradients. Steps follow that average.

quiz.q: With momentum 0.9, one very large wrong gradient arrives once. How does its influence on later steps behave?
options: It fades gradually over roughly 10 to 20 steps
It affects only the next step
quiz.why: Each step multiplies the old buffer by 0.9, so the large gradient fades over about 10 to 20 steps.

wrong.0: That would be no momentum at all; the buffer keeps a decaying share of the old value.

quiz.q: Why does momentum matter more at batch 16 than at batch 256?
options: Small batches give noisier gradients, and averaging removes noise
Momentum only works at small batch sizes
quiz.why: A small batch is a small sample of the data, so its gradient is the true direction plus a lot of noise. Averaging over about 10 steps removes much of it.

quiz.q: At momentum 0.9, by about what factor does averaging improve the signal-to-noise ratio if the true gradient stays steady?
quiz.why: The factor is sqrt((1 + 0.9)/(1 - 0.9)) = 4.4. It is an upper bound if the signal drifts within the window.

wrong.3: 10 is roughly how many steps are averaged, but recent steps count more than old ones, so the noise shrinks by less than 10 times. It works out to 4.4.

quiz.q: What is a cost of momentum?
options: It reacts late when the right direction changes
It increases the number of weights
quiz.why: The buffer remembers the old direction, so it lags for about 10 steps after a change.

plain: An orthogonal matrix turns or flips things without stretching any direction, so all of its directions are equally strong.
ours: Muon replaces the momentum matrix with an approximately orthogonal one before stepping. The gradient still decides which directions the matrix changes in, but every direction the method reaches gets a step of similar size, however faint the gradient was along it. 'Strong' means a lot of the gradient lies along that direction. In one of our heads, the momentum of an MLP matrix (1024 x 256) had a strongest direction about 10,000 times its weakest. After the update the strongest 100 or so directions sit between 0.7 and 1.2, and the weakest stay small.
deeper: For a gradient matrix G = U S V^T (S holds the strengths, called singular values), the nearest orthogonal matrix is U V^T: every strength is replaced by 1. Computing that exactly is expensive, so Muon runs five Newton-Schulz iterations, a fixed polynomial with coefficients (3.4445, -4.7750, 2.0315) chosen to put the strengths roughly between 0.7 and 1.3. The Muon post reports that this error does not hurt. Directions far weaker than the strongest are not pulled up within five steps. Textbook: the Muon post; ours: the same five iterations.

papers.title: Keller Jordan, Muon: An optimizer for hidden layers in neural networks
Moonlight: Muon is Scalable for LLM Training

quiz.q: What is special about an orthogonal matrix's directions?
options: They all point the same way
quiz.why: An orthogonal matrix does not stretch any direction: all strengths are 1.

quiz.q: Why does Muon orthogonalise its update?
options: So every direction gets a step of similar size, not just those with the largest gradient
quiz.why: Without it the biggest gradient directions dominate. Orthogonalising gives faint directions a real step too.

quiz.q: Muon uses five Newton-Schulz iterations rather than computing the exact orthogonal matrix. Why?
options: It is cheaper to run, and an approximate result does not hurt
Five is the number of layers
The exact result needs the data
It is required by the GPU
quiz.why: The exact decomposition is expensive on GPUs; a few matrix multiplications give a close-enough answer (the Muon post reports no harm).

quiz.q: After five iterations, how orthogonal is the result in practice?
options: Roughly: the strengths land between about 0.7 and 1.3
Only the weakest direction is fixed
Only the strongest direction is fixed
quiz.why: The coefficients trade exactness for speed, leaving the strengths between about 0.7 and 1.3.

quiz.q: A momentum matrix has a strongest direction 10,000 times its weakest. After five iterations, what happens to the weakest direction?
options: It becomes as strong as the strongest
It stays small, because five steps cannot lift something that faint
quiz.why: The iteration lifts moderately weak directions toward 1, but directions far weaker than the strongest remain small within five steps.

wrong.0: That is the ideal exact result; with five iterations it does not reach the faintest directions.

plain: The optimizer is the rule that decides, after each batch, how much to change every weight, given the gradients the batch produced.
ours: This guide compares AdamW, Muon and several variants of both, plus Lion. The optimizer we use for most heads is our own (a Muon-type optimizer built from published parts), and the guide says where a piece is a textbook implementation and where it is ours.
deeper: The loss says how wrong the model is; the gradient says which way to change each weight to make it less wrong; the optimizer turns that into an actual change. Two optimizers given the same gradients can produce very different weights, which is why the choice behaves like a style choice as well as a speed choice (our notes, TRAINING F6).

papers.title: Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization (AdamW)

quiz.q: What does an optimizer do?
options: It decides how to change the weights after each batch
It splits the data into batches
quiz.why: It turns gradients into weight changes.

quiz.q: Two optimizers see exactly the same gradients. Will they change the weights in the same way?
options: Not necessarily; the rule for using the gradients differs
Only if the learning rate is zero
quiz.why: The gradient only says which way is downhill; each optimizer has its own rule for how far and how, so the results can differ a lot.

quiz.q: According to our own training notes, which of these is a mistake to assume?
options: That matched loss means two optimizers are interchangeable
That the optimizer changes the weights
quiz.why: Our listening notes found that optimizers with matched loss can sound different (TRAINING F6), so matched loss does not make them interchangeable.

plain: For each weight, the gradient says which way and how strongly the loss would change if that weight were nudged; the optimizer steps the other way.
ours: We compute it on a batch of examples. A batch of 1 to 16 is a small sample of the data, so its gradient is the true direction plus a lot of noise. In a matrix, a gradient is 'strong' along a direction when a large share of its size lies along that direction, and 'weak' when little does. Our momentum matrices were dominated by some strong directions, with a long tail of faint ones.
deeper: The gradient is computed by backpropagation, one batch at a time. The noise level falls as the batch grows; our measurements of how much of a half-batch gradient agrees with the other half are in guide section 6. Gradient clipping caps its size so one huge value cannot cause a huge step.

quiz.q: What does a gradient tell the optimizer?
options: Which way to nudge each weight to reduce the loss, and how strongly
The final answer of the model
quiz.why: It is the local slope of the loss with respect to the weights.

quiz.q: Why is a gradient from a batch of 4 noisy?
options: It is computed on a small sample of the data
The learning rate is too low
quiz.why: Four examples are a small sample, so the gradient differs from the one the whole dataset would give.

quiz.q: In a gradient matrix, what does 'strong along a direction' mean?
options: A large share of the gradient's size lies along that direction
The direction has the largest learning rate
quiz.why: Strength is how much of the matrix is concentrated along one direction.

plain: The learning rate is the number that scales every step: the optimizer works out a direction and a size for the update, and the learning rate multiplies it.
ours: Our best head setting with AdamW was a learning rate of 3e-4. Our original Muon recipe's best was 1e-2, and the rescaled recipe's best was 3e-3. The numbers differ because the optimizers' updates have different built-in sizes, not because one is 'stronger'. One learning rate shared across different parameter groups gave different step sizes in each.
deeper: A learning rate is a scale, so the same number means different step sizes under different optimizers: about 0.2 to 0.4 of the learning rate per weight for AdamW, and a size set by the matrix shape for Muon (guide section 4). Training usually starts with a short warmup, then either decays the rate or uses Schedule-Free averaging. Too high a rate gives NaN or noisy runs; too low a rate learns too slowly.

quiz.q: What does the learning rate do?
options: It scales the size of every step
quiz.why: Step = learning rate times the optimizer's update.

quiz.q: Why can the same learning rate number be good for AdamW and bad for Muon?
options: Their updates have different built-in sizes
The numbers are in different units of time
quiz.why: Both multiply an update, but the update's own size differs, so the same number gives different steps.

quiz.q: A run goes NaN soon after training starts at a high learning rate. What is the most likely cause?
options: Steps were too large, so some values blew up
The learning rate was too low
quiz.why: Too-large steps can push weights or magnitudes out of range; the guide's runs B3 and the DoRA magnitude failures are examples.

quiz.q: One shared learning rate is applied to the matrices and to the biases. What may go wrong under a sign step?
options: The biases take much larger steps than the matrices
quiz.why: A sign step moves each bias by the full learning rate, far more than Muon moves a matrix weight, so biases can run away first.

plain: AdamW is the standard optimizer: it gives each weight its own step size, based on how large and how steady that weight's recent gradients were, and it applies weight decay separately from the gradient.
ours: We use it as the baseline and for the parts Muon cannot handle: biases, gains, magnitudes and other 1-D parameters. Adam and AdamW are two different optimizers that match only when weight decay is zero, so check which one a paper or a recipe means before comparing numbers.
deeper: Adam keeps two running averages per weight: of the gradient, and of its square. The step is the first divided by the square root of the second, times the learning rate. Adam adds weight decay into the gradient, where it gets divided like everything else; AdamW applies decay directly to the weights, which behaves more predictably.

quiz.q: What is AdamW in one sentence?
options: An optimizer that gives each weight its own step size from its recent gradients
quiz.why: It is the standard per-weight adaptive optimizer.

quiz.q: When are Adam and AdamW the same?
quiz.why: They differ only in how weight decay is applied, so with no decay they match.

quiz.q: What is the difference in how they apply weight decay?
options: Adam adds it into the gradient; AdamW applies it directly to the weights
They apply it to different data
quiz.why: In AdamW decay is decoupled from the adaptive scaling.

plain: Muon is an optimizer for 2-D weight matrices: it averages the gradients, then replaces that average with a matrix whose directions are all about equally strong before stepping.
ours: We use Muon-type optimizers for the matrices of our heads, with AdamW or a sign step for everything else. Muon is not one fixed recipe: the original post, Moonlight's rescaled version, and our own variant differ in step size and normalisation, which is why learning rates from one do not carry to another.
deeper: Each step does three things for a matrix: momentum averaging, orthogonalisation with five Newton-Schulz iterations, and a step of size set by the learning rate and the matrix shape. The original post introduced it in December 2024 with results on CIFAR-10 and GPT-2-sized models. Whether it helps fine-tuning at all is an open question (guide section 7).

papers.title: Keller Jordan, Muon: An optimizer for hidden layers in neural networks

quiz.q: What kind of parameters is Muon designed for?
quiz.why: Muon works on whole matrices; other parameters go to a second optimizer.

quiz.q: What are Muon's three steps?
options: Average the gradients, orthogonalise the result, take a step
quiz.why: Momentum, orthogonalisation, step.

quiz.q: Why can't you copy a Muon learning rate between the original recipe, Moonlight's version and ours?
quiz.why: The step sizes differ by recipe, so the same number moves the weights differently.

plain: A Newton-Schulz iteration is a short, fixed calculation, built only from matrix multiplications, that pushes a matrix a little closer to its nearest orthogonal matrix; Muon repeats it five times.
ours: Muon normalises the momentum matrix, then runs five rounds. After five rounds the strengths of the matrix's directions are between about 0.7 and 1.3, not exactly 1, and directions far weaker than the strongest are barely lifted. In the figure in guide section 2 the strongest ~100 directions end up between 0.7 and 1.2.
deeper: Each round computes A = X times X-transpose, then X <- a X + (b A + c A squared) X with a, b, c = 3.4445, -4.7750, 2.0315. These numbers are chosen to bring the strengths near 1 quickly, not to converge exactly. It is used because it only needs matrix multiplications, which GPUs do well. Textbook: the Muon post; ours: the same five rounds.

papers.title: Keller Jordan, Muon: An optimizer for hidden layers in neural networks

quiz.q: What is a Newton-Schulz iteration used for in Muon?
options: To push the momentum matrix toward an orthogonal one
quiz.why: It approximates the orthogonal matrix with a few multiplications.

quiz.q: Why does Muon use it instead of an exact calculation?
options: It needs only matrix multiplications, which GPUs do fast
quiz.why: The exact decomposition is slow on GPUs; the iteration is fast and close enough.

quiz.q: After five iterations, the matrix's strengths are...
quiz.why: The coefficients trade exactness for speed.

plain: A singular value is the strength of one direction of a matrix: how much the matrix stretches an input that points along that direction.
ours: Every matrix has as many singular values as its smaller side. In one of our heads the momentum of a 1024 x 256 matrix had 256 of them, the largest about 10,000 times the smallest. Muon tries to bring all of them to about 1.
deeper: Writing a matrix as G = U S V-transpose, U and V hold the directions and S holds the singular values. The nearest orthogonal matrix is U V-transpose, which is G with every singular value replaced by 1. A singular value near zero means the matrix barely responds along that direction.

quiz.q: What is a singular value?
options: The strength of one direction of a matrix
quiz.why: It says how much the matrix stretches along one direction.

quiz.q: A 1024 x 256 matrix has how many singular values?
quiz.why: A matrix has as many singular values as its smaller side.

quiz.q: What does Muon do to a matrix's singular values?
quiz.why: That is what makes the matrix orthogonal.

plain: A matrix does not treat all inputs alike: it responds strongly to some directions of its input space and weakly to others, and those directions are what 'directions' means in this guide.
ours: Picture a matrix as a machine that stretches some input directions a lot and others hardly at all. Muon keeps the gradient's directions but evens out how much the matrix moves along each. In our momentum matrices a few directions were hundreds or thousands of times stronger than the faintest ones.
deeper: Technically these are the singular directions, which come in pairs (an input-side one and an output-side one), each with a singular value giving its strength. 'The gradient is strong along a direction' means that direction has a large singular value in the gradient matrix.

quiz.q: In this guide, what is a 'direction' of a matrix?
options: An input direction the matrix responds to, strongly or weakly
quiz.why: A matrix stretches different input directions by different amounts.

quiz.q: Muon gives faint directions a step of similar size to strong ones. Without that, which directions would dominate the update?
options: The ones with the fewest weights
quiz.why: Raw gradient updates follow the strong directions.

quiz.q: Directions come in pairs. What does each pair carry?
options: An input side, an output side and a strength
A learning rate and a schedule
quiz.why: Each singular direction pairs an input vector, an output vector and a singular value.

plain: Direction rank is the position of a direction when all of a matrix's directions are lined up from the strongest (rank 1) to the weakest.
ours: It is the horizontal axis of the Newton-Schulz figure in guide section 2. The left of the plot is the strongest directions, the right is the faintest ones. The curve shows how strong each direction is before and after the five iterations.
deeper: Plotting strength against rank, instead of a list of numbers, makes it easy to see how steeply the strengths fall (here by a factor of about 10,000) and how far five iterations lift the middle of the range but not the tail.

quiz.q: In the figure, which direction has rank 1?
options: The first one written in the file
quiz.why: Ranks run from strongest to weakest.

quiz.q: What does a curve falling steeply along direction rank show?
options: A few directions are much stronger than the rest
quiz.why: A steep fall means a few dominant directions.

quiz.q: After five Newton-Schulz iterations, which part of the curve is still low?
options: The weakest directions at high rank
quiz.why: The iteration does not lift directions far weaker than the strongest.

plain: Weight decay pulls every weight a little toward zero on each step, which stops the weights from growing without limit.
ours: Our full fine-tune path once ran with a weight decay of zero. The weights grew, the latents the model produced grew with them, and the audible result was a drone under the music. AdamW runs with a decay of 0.01 on the same data stayed healthy. Moonlight uses 0.1 on the matrices and SF-NorMuon uses 0.05; none is applied to gains and biases.
deeper: The pull per step is the learning rate times the decay setting. At the point where this pull balances the growth from the steps themselves, the weights stop growing; that balance is what 'rotational equilibrium' describes, and noise matters because random steps add up differently from consistent ones. We have not measured that balance on our heads. One paper, Muon-SW, reports that with a constant decay Muon's weight norm shrinks steadily and proposes scaling the decay with the learning rate; read it for the exact rule, because the guide summarises it in one sentence. Under Schedule-Free, where the learning rate does not decay, that scaling has no effect.

options: Pulls every weight slightly toward zero each step
quiz.why: It shrinks the weights a little on every step.

quiz.q: Why did a weight decay of zero cause a drone in our full fine-tunes?
options: The weights and the latents the model produced kept growing
quiz.why: Without decay the weights grew, and the output level grew with them.

quiz.q: The pull toward zero per step is...
options: The learning rate times the decay setting
quiz.why: Decay is applied scaled by the learning rate.

quiz.why: It reports Moonlight's 0.1 and SF-NorMuon's 0.05 as published settings, not as tuned results for our heads.

plain: The weight norm is a single number for the overall size of a group of weights; a steadily rising weight norm means the weights are growing.
ours: The guide asks you to log the average size of the weights in each parameter group every few hundred steps. A group whose size doubles within an epoch after warmup needs attention: in every failure we describe, the weights grew before the loss showed a problem. Our head trainer can halve that group's learning rate automatically; the option is new and off by default.
deeper: Weight growth can hide because the loss often stays normal while the weights grow: when a normalisation layer follows a matrix, the output depends on direction, not overall size, so growth changes the effective step size and eventually numerics before it changes the loss. 'Fixing the norm' is what Hyperball does; we found it is not a drop-in for adapters, because a matrix that starts at zero has norm zero and does not move.

quiz.why: The norm measures the overall size.

It is required by the GPU

plain: Schedule-Free is a way of training without lowering the learning rate over time: it keeps a running average of the weights and uses that average as the result.
ours: It was the largest single effect we measured on the heads: held-out loss 0.20 to 0.21 with it and 0.255 without, against 0.25 to 0.26 for AdamW (12,524 crops). It moves the weights quickly early, so epochs 2 to 4 can be the good ones when listening to a LoRA or DoRA. Its burn-in and averaging weight changed results by only 0.0005 to 0.006, which we treat as noise.
deeper: Instead of a decaying schedule, it evaluates and saves the average of the weights instead of the latest weights. Because the learning rate does not decay, a rule that scales weight decay with the learning rate has no effect under it. Its average is also affected by bf16 rounding when the steps are small. Published: The Road Less Scheduled, SF-NorMuon (the spectral version), and ScheduleFree+.

quiz.why: It removes the need to schedule the learning rate downward.

quiz.q: Which weights does a Schedule-Free run give you?
options: A running average of the weights
quiz.why: The saved model is the average, not the latest point.

quiz.q: Why did the guide say epochs 2 to 4 may be the good ones with Schedule-Free?
options: It moves the weights quickly early in training
It needs a warmup of 100 epochs

plain: A sign step moves each parameter by exactly the learning rate, up or down depending only on the sign of its gradient, however large or small the gradient was.
ours: Our own optimizer used a sign step for the 1-D parameters: each bias and gain moved by the full learning rate every step. That is why a shared learning rate made them take much larger steps than the matrices (about 1e-2 against 6e-4 per step in our original recipe), and why DoRA magnitudes, which started around 0.13 to 0.45, crossed zero.
deeper: Lion is the best-known optimizer built on this idea. A fixed step is blind to the size of a parameter, so it is a poor fit for small positive values such as DoRA magnitudes: 592 of them reached zero or below by step 6,340, and the run became NaN near step 6,900. A multiplicative update of the magnitudes fixed it. We have not checked whether that fix appears in the literature.

quiz.q: How big is a sign step?
options: Always the learning rate, whatever the gradient's size
quiz.why: Only the sign of the gradient is used.

options: Fixed-size steps can push small positive numbers below zero
quiz.why: A step comparable to the value itself can cross zero.

quiz.q: Which optimizer is best known for using the sign of the gradient?
quiz.why: Lion uses the sign of the momentum.

wrong.1: Muon orthogonalises the momentum matrix, which is not a sign step.
wrong.3: AdamW divides by the root of the averaged squared gradient, which is not a sign step.

plain: NorMuon is a Muon variant that rescales every row of the update to a similar size after orthogonalising, so no row moves much more than the others.
ours: In our version, row normalisation cancels any overall size set before it, including the shape-based radius, so those settings have no effect while it is on. On wide matrices, including LoRA A, our variant steps 2 to 3.6 times larger than the reference implementation, and we have not traced why. We have no outcome test of it yet.
deeper: After Newton-Schulz the rows of an orthogonalised matrix can still differ in size. NorMuon divides each row by a running estimate of its size. Because it fixes the scale itself, any scale applied earlier is erased. Textbook: the NorMuon paper; ours: a variant whose step size differs from it.
